00Exam snapshot

Chapter 15 carries about 15 marks, the most in the exam. Case questions hand you a chart and ask which statement is "most likely true" or "not likely true". Learn the numbers below cold; most wrong options change exactly one of them.

NumberRuleWhere
RSI 70 / 30Above 70 overbought, below 30 oversold15.9.3
RSI 44–45Bull market floor: RSI rarely falls below this15.9.3
RSI 50–55Bear market ceiling: RSI rarely rises above this15.9.3
RSI 0–100Bounded. Never above 10015.9.3
MACD = 26 EMA − 12 EMAFast (default) line. Slow line = 9 EMA of the fast line15.9.2
MACD zero lineSeparates confirmed bull from confirmed bear. A zero-line crossover is not a trading signal15.9.2
ADX 25 / 14 barsBelow 25 weak or no trend; rising above 25 strong trend. Default period 1415.9.4
EMA 13 / 21 / 34Fibonacci set. Bull: price takes support at 34 EMA. Bear: price resists at 34 EMA15.9.1
OBV 1 vs OBV 20OBV line read against its 20-period average15.9.6
RSC 100 / 5–6 yrsAbove 100 outperforming the benchmark; calculate over 5–6 years15.9.5
Shadow ≥ 2x bodyHammer and hanging man15.5.1–2
4+ red candlesBullish engulfing more reliable after these15.5.3
50% of prior bodyDark cloud closes below midpoint; piercing covers at least half15.5.5–6
2 points (3+ better)Minimum for a trendline15.8
1/3 to 2/3 retracementSecondary trend retraces this much of the primary move (Dow)15.4.2
10–20%Typical bull-market correction15.4.2
38.2 / 50 / 61.8%Fibonacci retracement reversal zones15.4.2
Golden rule for case questions. A signal counts only with confirmation: volume, a confirming candle, ADX above 25, or a higher timeframe agreeing. Options that act on an unconfirmed signal are usually the wrong ones.

15.1Introduction and assumptions

Technical analysis studies price and volume from trading activity, assuming all relevant information is already in the price.

#AssumptionMeaning
iPrice discounts everythingAll known and unknown information (economic, political, psychological) is in the price. Analysts look only at price and volume
iiPrice moves in trendsUp, down or sideways. An established trend is more likely to continue than reverse
iiiHistory repeats itselfBehaviour is cyclical and driven by psychology; patterns recur
ivMarket action is predictable (to a degree)Probabilistic, not guaranteed. TA is about managing risk
vVolume confirms priceHigh volume on breakouts or reversals adds credibility

Technical vs fundamental

FeatureTechnicalFundamental
FocusPrice action, market behaviourIntrinsic value
DataHistoric price and volumeFinancial statements, economic and industry reports
HorizonShort / medium-term tradingLong-term investing
ToolsChart patterns, RSI, MAs, MACD, OBVCash flows, DCF, SWOT, ratios
AssumptionPrice captures all information; trend continuesPrice can deviate from intrinsic value
ObjectiveForecast price moves, trading opportunitiesFind under- or overvalued assets
Followed byTraders, chartists, speculatorsFund managers, value and long-term investors

15.2Chart types

ChartBuilt fromIgnoresBest for
LineClosing prices joinedOpen, high, low (intraday)Quick trend view, long-term perspective
Bar (OHLC)Open, High, Low, Close—Detailed price action, volatility, range and directional bias
CandlestickOHLC as coloured candles—Patterns (Doji, Hammer, Engulfing), market psychology
Point & FigureX (up) and O (down) columnsTime and volumeBreakout levels, support/resistance, long-term trend
RenkoFixed-size bricksTimeTrend clarity, momentum, trailing stops
Heikin-AshiAveraged candlesRaw noiseTrend-following; staying in a trade through whipsaws
How to read it
  • Only closing prices are joined, so the path is clean and the big trend jumps out: a low near 17,250 in early 2023, a steady climb to about 26,250 by Sep 2024, a dip, then recovery to 25,709.
  • Green segments are up-moves, red are down-moves. You cannot see any day's high, low or gaps.
  • The panel below shows volume with its average; the bottom line is a relative-strength line hovering near 100.
Exam angleLine charts answer "which way is the trend?" only. Any question about candles, gaps or wicks needs a bar or candlestick chart.
How to read it
  • Each vertical bar spans the period's high to low. The small left tick is the open; the right tick is the close.
  • Right tick above left tick (green) = closed higher. Right tick below left (red) = closed lower.
  • Long bars show high volatility. In June, a run of red bars with lower closes takes price from about $70 to under $10; July has a similar fall, then a run of green bars to about $85.
Exam angleBar and candlestick charts carry the same four data points. Candlesticks just make open versus close easier to see.
How to read it
  • Body = open to close. Green (hollow) closed above the open; red closed below. Wicks show the high and low.
  • On 24 Oct a long red candle drops price from about 2,706 to 2,698: strong selling.
  • Next come tiny bodies around 2,700 (doji-like): indecision, with sellers unable to push lower.
  • By 26 Oct a series of green candles lifts price back to 2,708.
Exam angleLong body = conviction. Tiny body with wicks = indecision, often at a turning point.
How to read it
  • X columns are rising prices; O columns are falling prices. A new column starts only when price reverses by a set amount, so there is no time axis.
  • Each new X column here tops out higher than the last, and O columns stop at higher levels: an uptrend.
  • A buy signal is an X column breaking above the previous X column's top.
Exam angleP&F ignores both time and volume — a favourite trick option.
How to read it
  • A new brick is drawn only when price moves a fixed amount. Green bricks rise, red bricks fall; the x-axis is not evenly spaced in time.
  • Clear trends: a fall from about 126 to 112, then a steady run of green bricks back to 122.
  • Small moves smaller than a brick never appear, which filters noise. A colour change marks a reversal and is where a trailing stop sits.
Exam angleRenko ignores time. Use it for trend clarity and trailing stops.
How to read it
  • Candles use averaged prices, so they come in smooth runs of one colour.
  • Long run of green candles with no lower wick = strong uptrend.
  • Circled: the first small red candle at the top. That is the early warning.
  • What follows is a string of large red candles with no upper wicks = strong downtrend. Trend-followers stay short until candles shrink and wicks appear on both sides.
Exam angleHeikin-Ashi values are averages, not real OHLC prices. It keeps you in a trend by filtering whipsaws.

15.3Dow Theory

Charles Dow wrote the editorials (1900–1902). William Hamilton and Robert Rhea formalised them after his death.

#TenetKey point
iMarket discounts everythingEconomic, political and psychological information is in the price. Aligns with EMH
iiMarket has three trendsPrimary, secondary, tertiary
iiiPrimary trend has three phasesAccumulation (smart money enters quietly) → public participation (momentum builds) → distribution (smart money exits; retail late). Mirrors Wyckoff's cycle
ivIndices must confirm each otherBoth major indices move the same way, e.g. Nifty and Sensex. Used in intermarket analysis
vVolume confirms the trendVolume rises in the direction of the primary trend
viTrends persist until a clear reversalBasis of trend-following, trailing stops and MA crossovers
Workbook sample Q1: "Which is NOT a tenet?" Answer: the market has four trends. It has three.

15.4Market trends

TrendDurationWhat it isTools
PrimaryOne year or moreDominant long-term direction: bull, bear or sideways50/100 DMA, trendlines, MACD, HH/HL or LH/LL structure
Secondary3 weeks – 3 monthsMoves against the primary: correction in a bull, rally in a bear. Retraces 1/3 to 2/3 of the primary move; lower volumeFibonacci (38.2/50/61.8%), 50 DMA, volume, RSI/stochastic
TertiaryUnder 3 weeks (some say up to 6)Short swings; can go with or against bigger trends; reverses quickly5/10/20-day EMA, RSI, stochastic, candles, pivots

Primary trend types

TypeDescriptionSentiment
BullSustained rise driven by optimism, growth, liquidityConfidence, expansion
BearProlonged decline, often economic contraction or crisisFear, contraction
SidewaysHorizontal rangeNeutral, uncertain

Drivers of primary trends: economic cycles, monetary policy, fiscal policy, geopolitics, investor psychology. Bull markets favour breakout buying and growth stocks; bear markets favour defensives, hedging and short selling.

Secondary trend details

ItemDetail
Names"Pullbacks" in bull markets, "relief rallies" in bear markets
PurposeDigest gains/losses, shake out weak hands, reset overbought/oversold
TriggersMacro data, central bank shifts, geopolitics, earnings surprises, technical exhaustion (overbought RSI, divergence)
Case: Nifty 2020–21Primary bullish post-COVID; Sep–Oct 2020 correction of about 7% on global risk-off; uptrend resumed to new highs by early 2021

Tertiary trend: uses and risks

UsesRisks
Fine-tune entries/exits; tight stop-losses; read sentiment; building blocks of flags, pennants, wedgesNoise vs signal in choppy markets; whipsaws and false breakouts; overtrading costs

15.5Candlestick reversal patterns

The same shape means different things depending on what came before. Always check the prior trend first, then wait for confirmation.

PatternCandlesAfterSignalRule to remember
Hanging man1Up moveBearishSmall body, lower shadow ≥ 2x body, little/no upper shadow. Next candle must close lower
Hammer1DeclineBullishSame shape. Tail ≥ 2x body. Price must move up next (confirmation)
Bullish engulfing2DeclineBullishLarge green body fully engulfs prior red body. Stronger after 4+ red candles
Bearish engulfing2Advance (most significant)BearishRed body engulfs green body. Real bodies only, both long; ignore in choppy markets
Dark cloud cover2Uptrend, top of congestionBearishGap up opens, turns red, closes below midpoint of prior green
Piercing2Downtrend, bottom of congestionBullishGap down opens, green covers at least half of prior red
Morning star3DowntrendBullishTall red → small body with long wicks → tall green
Evening star3UptrendBearishLarge green → small body closing above it → large red closing near centre of first body

A congestion area is a price range where the market trades repeatedly for several weeks before breaking out up or down.

How to read it
  • Four green candles climb: an up move.
  • Circled "T" candle at the top: small body high up, long lower shadow. Sellers controlled part of the session.
  • The next candle closes lower (red). That confirms it; the dashed line shows the downtrend that follows.
Exam angleIt is only a warning until the next candle closes lower. Traders exit longs during or after the confirmation candle, not before.
How to read it
  • Several red candles fall: a decline.
  • Circled candle: small green body with a long lower shadow. Sellers pushed price down but buyers brought it back near the open.
  • The next candles are green and rising: confirmation. Entry is taken after that candle.
Exam angleSame shape as the hanging man. Location decides the meaning: after a fall = hammer (bullish); after a rise = hanging man (bearish).
How to read it
  • A string of red candles marks the downtrend.
  • Circled pair: small red, then a larger green whose body wraps around it.
  • The chart marks entry above the green candle, a stop-loss below the pattern's low, and a take-profit target. Price climbs to that target.
Exam angleReliability rises when four or more red candles come before it.
How to read it
  • A steady uptrend of green candles.
  • Circled pair at the top: a green candle, then a larger red candle whose body engulfs it.
  • Stop-loss sits above the pattern high; entry below the red candle. Price then falls to the take-profit line.
Exam angleCompare bodies only, not wicks. Two small candles make a weak signal.
How to read it
  • Uptrend into a highlighted peak.
  • Highlighted pair: a strong green candle, then a red candle that opens higher and closes below the middle of the green body.
  • After it, price makes lower highs and lower lows for the rest of the chart.
Exam angleMust close below the 50% point. Closing below the whole body would make it a bearish engulfing instead.
How to read it
  • Arrow shows the downtrend.
  • Circled pair: a red candle, then a green candle opening lower but closing above the red body's midpoint.
  • A sharp rally follows, shown by the rising arrow.
Exam angleTwo candles, near the bottom of a congestion area. Workbook sample Q3 tests exactly this.
How to read it
  • Downtrend into the circled three-candle group.
  • Tall red, then a tiny "star" candle (indecision), then a tall green.
  • Entry level is drawn above the third candle; stop-loss below the star's low. A new uptrend follows.
Exam angleThe third candle confirms the reversal.
How to read it
  • Strong uptrend into the shaded box.
  • Large green, then a small candle at the top, then a large red that opens below it and closes deep into the first body.
  • Price then trends lower for weeks.
Exam angleMirror of the morning star: bearish, at a top.

15.6Consolidation (continuation) patterns

PatternShapeUsually inBiasTrade
Symmetrical triangleLower highs + higher lowsAny trendNeutral until breakLong on break above, short below. Also called a wedge
Ascending triangleFlat resistance + higher lowsUptrendBullish continuationLong above resistance; short below lower trendline
Descending triangleLower highs + flat supportDowntrendBearish continuationShort on breakdown
FlagRectangle, sideways/slightly down, after sharp rallyUptrendBullish continuationLong on break above upper line
PennantSmall triangle after sharp rallyUptrendBullish continuationSame as flag

Rules. Triangle lines need at least two swing highs and two swing lows. Target = height at the thickest point, added to or subtracted from the breakout point. The sharp move before a flag/pennant is the flagpole.

How to read it
  • Peak near $390 in early Sep, then lower highs (upper line slopes down) and higher lows from about $200 (lower line slopes up).
  • Price squeezes into a narrowing range through Oct and early Nov.
  • Mid-Nov it breaks above the upper line near $330 and runs past $450, then above $700 in Dec.
  • Target check: thickest height about $390 − $200 = $190; breakout $330 + $190 ≈ $520. It was exceeded.
Exam angleDirection is decided by the break, not the shape.
How to read it
  • Uptrend first, then price keeps hitting the same flat resistance.
  • Each pullback ends higher (rising lower trendline): buyers are getting stronger.
  • Price finally breaks above the flat line: long trade, target = triangle height added to the breakout.
Exam angleFlat top + rising bottom = bullish.
How to read it
  • 1: downtrend. 2: consolidation. 3: flat lower support. 4: falling upper trendline (lower highs).
  • 5: price breaks below the flat support and the downtrend continues.
Exam angleFlat bottom + falling top = bearish. Short on the breakdown.
How to read it
  • Mid-May: a near-vertical jump of about 10 points on a large volume spike — the flagpole.
  • Late May to June: price drifts slightly down inside two parallel green lines — the flag. Volume dries up.
  • Late June: breakout above the flag. The second "10" marks the measured move: flagpole height added to the breakout, which is reached in July.
Exam angleVolume high on the pole, low in the flag, rising again on the breakout.

15.7Support and resistance

Support is a floor from concentrated demand. Resistance is a ceiling from concentrated supply. Both are zones, not exact prices.

TypeDescriptionExample
HorizontalFlat level where price repeatedly reversesXYZ resisting near Rs 1,950
TrendlineDiagonal line on higher lows / lower highsRising support in a bull trend
Moving averageDynamic levelBounce off 50 DMA
FibonacciRetracement ratios 23.6 / 38.2 / 61.8%Stock retracing 23.6% from swing high
Pivot pointsFrom prior period's high, low, closeIntraday trading
PsychologicalRound numbersNifty 25,000
ConceptDetail
Why they matterTraders remember reversal levels; orders cluster there; they define stop-loss and take-profit; breaks/bounces confirm direction
Role reversalBroken support becomes resistance (and vice versa): trapped traders exit at breakeven, sentiment shifts, institutions reposition
BreakoutDecisive move beyond the level with volume
False breakoutBrief breach that quickly reverses, trapping traders
Identify withSwing highs/lows, consolidation zones, MACD, Bollinger Bands, RSI, double tops/bottoms, head and shoulders, triangles, volume, multi-timeframe
StrategiesBounce (buy support, sell resistance); breakout with volume; pullback entry on retest; stop just below support / above resistance
LimitationsZones not exact; subjective; less respected in trends; news overrides them
AdvancedOrder blocks, liquidity pools (stop clusters), VWAP, anchored VWAP
CaseNifty support near 24,350 (May–Sep 2025). Reliance resistance near 1,300 (Oct 2021–Jul 2023), broke out Jan 2024

Strength of a level

FactorStronger when
TouchesMore touches
VolumeHigher volume at the level
TimeLonger consolidation near it
RecencyMore recent
How to read it
  • Red band on top = resistance; blue band at the bottom = support. Price swings between them for the whole chart.
  • Count the touches: about five at each band, which makes both levels strong.
  • Near the middle, price dips well below support for a few candles and then recovers — a false breakdown that trapped sellers.
  • At the far right, price pokes above resistance and drops back: a failed breakout.
Exam angleIn a range, buy near support and sell near resistance. Trust a break only with volume and a close beyond the zone.

15.8Trendlines and channels

ItemRule
TrendlineStraight line through 2+ points, extended forward as support/resistance. 3+ points = more reliable
Up / down / flatRising through higher lows = bullish; falling through lower highs = bearish; sideways = consolidation
DrawingWicks or closes depending on strategy; adjust as new data arrives
ChannelTwo parallel lines. Start with a valid trendline, draw parallel from the opposite swing point. Width = volatility
Channel typesAscending (HH/HL, bullish), descending (LH/LL, bearish), horizontal (rangebound)
CategoryItemMeaning
Trendline strategyBounceEnter on touch with confirmation (e.g. bullish candle)
Trendline strategyBreakoutEnter on decisive break with volume
Trendline strategyTrailing stopTrail stop along the line
Channel strategyRange tradingBuy lower boundary, sell upper
Channel strategyBreakoutEnter on breakout with retest confirmation
Channel strategyWidth targetingProject the channel height from the breakout
ValidationVolume / candles / indicators / timeframeRising volume; engulfing, hammer, shooting star at the line; RSI divergence, MACD crossovers; higher-timeframe lines weigh more
PitfallForcing lines / ignoring breaks / overrelianceFitting lines to bias; not redrawing after invalidation; no confirmation from other tools
How to read it
  • Left half: red ascending channel. Price makes higher highs and higher lows between two parallel lines.
  • Inside it, short black down-sloping channels are the pullbacks; each ends at the lower red line, which is where range traders buy.
  • Mid-chart: price breaks below the red channel's lower line. The uptrend is over.
  • Right half: blue descending channel. The small black up-sloping channels inside it are counter-rallies (bear flags), each failing at the upper blue line.
  • Far right: price breaks below the blue channel and falls faster.
Exam angleSmall counter-trend channels inside a big channel are entry points in the direction of the big channel.
How to read it
  • 2021 to late 2023: price swings roughly between 1,100 and 1,400. The 13/21/34 EMAs keep crossing each other — no clear trend.
  • Rising lows in 2023 form an uptrend line; a parallel line from swing highs gives an ascending channel.
  • Late 2023 into early 2024: price breaks above the channel to about 1,566. Volume bars jump, the EMAs fan out in bull order (price > 13 > 21 > 34).
  • RSI climbs above 75 (overbought, normal in a strong breakout). MACD rises well above its signal line and above zero.
Exam angleBreakout + volume + aligned EMAs + rising MACD = bullish continuation.

15.9.1Moving averages

RuleDetail
WhatSmoothed average of daily/weekly/monthly closes. Lagging, but good for major trends
DirectionMA pointing up = uptrend. Daily, weekly and monthly MAs aligned = strong chance of continuation
Buy zonePrice at or near a rising MA
Fibonacci set13, 21, 34 EMA
UptrendPrice > 13 > 21 > 34 EMA; support near 34 EMA. All rising and spreading apart = strong bull
DowntrendPrice < 13 < 21 < 34 EMA; resistance near 34 EMA. All falling and spreading = strong selling
How to read it
  • Aug–Oct 2023: price flat near 620–650; the three EMAs are tangled. No trend.
  • From Nov: price stays above the 13 EMA (purple), which stays above the 21 (green), above the 34 (black). Textbook bull order.
  • The EMAs rise and spread apart into Feb 2024 — trend is strengthening. Price reaches about 1,060.
  • March pullback: price drops to the EMA band near 940–965 (around the 34 EMA), finds support and turns up again.
Exam angleIn a bull market, the 34 EMA is the support to watch.
How to read it
  • Peak near 4,400 in Aug–Sep 2021. By early 2022 the EMAs flip to bear order: price < 13 < 21 < 34.
  • Through 2022 into May 2023, every rally stalls at or below the black 34 EMA — the resistance in a downtrend. Price falls to about 1,000.
  • Jul 2023: a big green candle on high volume jumps above all three EMAs. They flatten and cross: momentum shifting.
  • Late 2023 to Mar 2024: price hovers around 1,755 with EMAs intertwined — base-building, not yet a confirmed uptrend.
Exam angleBear order + rallies failing at 34 EMA = stay away. EMAs tangling after a long fall = possible base.

15.9.2MACD

RuleDetail
ConstructionFast (default) line = 26 EMA − 12 EMA. Slow line = 9 EMA of the fast line
MeasuresMomentum, not price. Use with price action and other indicators
BuyWith both lines rising, fast crosses above slow. Or fast already above slow makes a fresh upturn after nearly touching it
Trend in forceFast above slow, both rising; lines keep a constant gap
Leading behaviourPrice higher high + MACD lower high = losing upward momentum. Price new low + MACD higher low = likely bottoming
Zero lineSeparates confirmed bull from confirmed bear. Do not trade the zero-line crossover
SteepnessSteep = powerful move; shallow = weak
Buying climaxFast line bulging far above slow → sideways market or mild correction
False signalsMACD can flatten or turn after a strong move without a trend reversal — only losing speed
ReversalMACD double top or double bottom
FilterAvoid stocks whose weekly or monthly MACD is clearly trending down
RangeUnbounded — not 0 to 100
How to read it
  • 2020 to Jan 2022: price runs from about 600 to 1,900. The MACD lines (bottom panel) climb steeply and stay far above zero — a powerful, confirmed bull trend.
  • Early 2022: the fast line crosses below the slow line and both fall; price drops toward 1,350.
  • Mid-2022 to 2023: MACD sinks below zero (confirmed bear phase) while price grinds to about 1,200.
  • Late 2023: lines cross back up and rise above zero; price recovers to about 1,750.
  • At the right edge, both lines are rolling over while price slips to 1,479 — momentum is fading.
Exam angleA falling higher-timeframe MACD is a reason to avoid the stock, even if price still looks fine.
How to read it
  • 2015–2020: long base between about 20 and 60. MACD lines are flat near zero.
  • From 2021: price begins a steady climb. Fast line stays above slow, both rising, and the gap widens.
  • 2023–24: steep, parabolic move to 224.50. MACD is at its steepest — a powerful move.
  • RSI holds above 70 for months: overbought can persist in a strong trend.
Exam angleRising weekly MACD with a steady gap = trend in force. A later bulge far above the slow line warns of a buying climax.

15.9.3RSI

RuleValue
MeasuresSpeed and magnitude of recent price changes. Oscillator 0–100
Best inTrading range markets. Can act as a lead indicator
Overbought / oversoldAbove 70 / below 30
Bull market floorRarely below 44–45
Bear market ceilingRarely above 50–55
PersistenceCan stay above 70 for long in a strong bull; below 30 in an extreme bear
Bullish divergenceOversold; price new low, RSI not — early buy
Bearish divergenceOverbought; price new high, RSI not — early sell
Workbook sample Q5: stock makes a new low and RSI does not = bullish divergence. The trap options call it bearish, or claim RSI works best in strongly trending markets.
How to read it
  • Early 2023: Nifty bottoms near 17,000. EMAs flip into bull order and fan out through 2023–24.
  • RSI (middle panel) spends most of Dec 2023 – Sep 2024 between about 60 and 75 and never drops near 44: textbook bull-market behaviour.
  • Sep 2024: Nifty makes its high near 26,250, but RSI and MACD peak lower than earlier — bearish divergence.
  • Oct 2024: MACD fast line crosses below slow, then falls below zero by early 2025. Price corrects to about 22,000 (Mar 2025); RSI dips close to 40.
  • Apr 2025: MACD crosses back up; price recovers to 25,709 but RSI only near 55–60 and MACD near zero — a much weaker trend than 2024.
Exam angleThis is the same chart as the workbook case study. Practise reading it until each answer below feels obvious.

15.9.4ADX

RuleDetail
MeasuresTrend strength, never direction. Based on a moving average of price-range expansion
Setting / rangeDefault 14 bars; single line 0–100. Works on stocks, MFs, ETFs, futures
Companions+DMI and −DMI (direction)
LevelsBelow 25 weak/no trend. Rising, especially above 25 = strong trend
Buy+DMI crosses above −DMI and ADX rising
Sell+DMI crosses below −DMI and ADX rising
AvoidDMI crossovers when ADX is weak — trade unlikely to succeed
How to read it
  • Apr–Aug 2025: price chops between about 960 and 1,060. The blue ADX line stays low (under 20–25) and DMI lines keep crossing: no trend, so crossovers are ignored.
  • From Sep 2025: green +DMI stays above red −DMI, and blue ADX starts rising past 25 toward 30+.
  • That combination is the buy signal. Price breaks out and climbs to 1,163 with EMAs in bull order.
Exam angleWorkbook text: blue = ADX (rising from Sep 2025), green = DMI+, red = DMI−. Buy when DMI+ crosses over DMI− and ADX starts moving up.

15.9.5RSC — Relative Strength Comparative

RuleDetail
Also calledRelative Strength Indicator, Price Relative Indicator
HowRatio chart of one security vs another (e.g. Nifty 50), normalised to 100, over 5–6 years
UsesVs benchmark; vs sector peers; find stocks that hold up in falls or lag in rallies
ReadAbove 100 outperforming; below 100 underperforming
Good buyBelow 100 for a long time, then turns up and crosses 100

15.9.6OBV — On Balance Volume

SignalCondition
BuildClose up: add day's volume. Close down: subtract it
NormalOBV rises with price and falls with price. In a divergence, volume precedes price
Very bullishOBV 1 zigzags up above a steadily rising OBV 20 (weekly/monthly)
Very bearishOBV 1 zigzags down below a falling OBV 20
BuyOBV 1 crosses rising OBV 20 upward; or OBV 1 above OBV 20 makes a fresh upturn
SellOBV 1 crosses falling OBV 20 downward
Strong uptrendBoth lines rounding upward for a long time
Buying climaxOBV 1 bulges far above OBV 20
Early reversalPronounced weakening of long-term OBV — smart money exiting quietly
Fading buyingPrice higher high without a higher OBV 1
ConfirmationWeekly and daily OBV should confirm a monthly OBV buy signal
How to read it
  • Early 2023: price falls to about 1,500 and the RSC line (third panel) sits below 100 — underperforming Nifty.
  • Mid-2023: RSC turns up and crosses 100. That is the RSC buy signal.
  • OBV (bottom panel) rises above its average and keeps climbing. Volume supports the move.
  • Price climbs to 5,715 by Oct 2025 with EMAs in bull order; RSC near 150, i.e. strongly outperforming.
Exam angleRSC crossing 100 after a long time below + OBV rising = high-quality buy.
How to read it
  • From May 2023, the OBV line (bottom panel) starts rising steadily above its average.
  • Price follows: from about 4,000–5,000 to about 17,000–18,000 — roughly 4x.
  • The RSC line (third panel) also rises well above 100: outperforming the benchmark throughout.
  • OBV rose before the big price moves, showing volume leading price.
Exam angleWorkbook fact: OBV turned up from May 2023; stock delivered 4x after that.

CSWorkbook case: Ankit Singh, Nifty weekly (Dec 2022 – Oct 2025)

Nifty bottomed near 16,900 in Mar 2023, rallied to a peak in Sep 2024, then traded sideways with a negative bias for over a year. Ankit uses RSI and MACD together.

How to read it
  • Rally phase (Mar 2023 – Sep 2024): EMAs stacked up, RSI mostly 60–75, MACD fast above slow and well above zero.
  • Sep 2024 top: new price high, but MACD (and RSI) peak lower than earlier — negative divergence.
  • Oct 2024: MACD fast line crosses below the slow line — a sell, not a buy.
  • Early 2025: correction to about 22,000, RSI near 40, MACD below zero.
  • Apr 2025 onward: recovery to 25,868; RSI 55–60, MACD hugging zero — sideways, weaker momentum.
Exam angleRead the four answers below against these points.
QAsksAnswerWhy the others fail
1RSI — most likely true(b) Dec 23 – Sep 24 strong trend, RSI remains overbought(a) Feb 2025 and (c) Sep 2023 divergences aren't on the chart; (d) RSI can't exceed 100
2RSI — NOT likely true(a) RSI can fall below 40 in a strong bull marketBull-market RSI rarely goes below 44–45. (b), (c), (d) are all true
3MACD — most likely true(a) Sep 24 high without MACD high = negative divergence(b) zero-line crossover is not a trade signal; (c) MACD isn't bounded 0–100; (d) MACD is not "generally" a lead indicator
4MACD — NOT likely true(d) MACD gave a buy signal in first week of Oct 2024Oct 2024 was a bearish crossover after the top. (a), (b), (c) are workbook rules

Workbook sample questions

QTopicAnswer
1NOT a Dow tenet(b) Market has four trends
2Hanging man is UNLIKELY to(d) Be a bullish reversal after a down move

4Default MACD line(c) 26 EMA and 12 EMA
5RSI most likely true(b) New low, RSI doesn't = bullish divergence

How to read any case chart

  1. Trend: are price and the 13/21/34 EMAs stacked up, down or tangled?
  2. RSI: compare with 70/30, the 44–45 bull floor and 50–55 bear ceiling.
  3. Divergence: compare price peaks/troughs with RSI, MACD and OBV peaks/troughs.
  4. MACD: which way did fast cross slow, and are both lines rising or falling?
  5. Confirmation: volume, candle, ADX above 25, higher timeframe.

A3Annexure 3 — Case studies from market history

Case 1: Barings (Nick Leeson)

ItemDetail
WhoNick Leeson, head of derivatives trading at Barings Futures Singapore — controlled both front and back office
TradeProprietary Nikkei 225 futures and options on SGX-DT (ex-SIMEX) and Osaka (OSE). Sold large short straddles — a bet the market stays stable
TriggerKobe earthquake: Nikkei fell, straddles lost money. He bought huge Nikkei futures to "support" the index — and failed
Cover storyTold London it was arbitrage between SGX-DT and OSE; told each exchange he had opposite positions on the other. Exchanges, competing for business, didn't cross-check
OutcomeBarings collapsed. Both exchanges stayed safe thanks to proper margining
#Lesson
1A single operator can't move the market. He should have cut losses on the short puts instead of buying futures
2Clearly defined, well-communicated position limits for every trader
3Meticulous monitoring of limits; separate front and back office; systems should block trades beyond limits
4Exchanges should share information on large positions
5Big institutions are as prone to risk as individuals — collect margins from all, on time. SEBI made margins universal for all participants including institutions
Conclusion to remember: "Barings' failure was not the derivatives failure, it was management's failure." The Board of Banking Supervision blamed poor operational controls (operational risk). Lessons 1–3 are for trading firms; lesson 4 is for exchanges.

Case 2: Credit event of 2008

StageWhat happened
Bank strategyLend to less creditworthy borrowers; loosen LTV from 80:20 to 85:15; higher rates lift NIMs
Borrower logicIf prices rise, sell and repay with profit; if prices fall, hand the keys to the bank
SecuritisationBanks originated mortgages and sold them to funds, which resold them — "passing the pillow". Last holders were stuck as prices fell to cents on the dollar
RatingsAgencies rated mortgage-backed securities AAA, relying on history and hard-asset backing; investors relied on those ratings
DerivativesMany credit derivatives written on these securities, for trading and hedging
Lesson
Banks are leveraged: lend with discipline, don't bet on asset prices, never dilute risk management to win business
Investors: do independent due diligence beyond ratings; keep asking "what could go wrong here"
History alone can't drive decisions; analyse the current situation with facts
No rating agency owned responsibility despite AAA ratings
Respect the limits of understanding — Taleb's Black Swans; risk management is paramount
